artworks.title: Odysseus and Eurycleia
artworks.description: Tischbein's Neoclassical painting isolates the Odyssey's most intimate recognition: Eurycleia washes the feet of the disguised Odysseus and sees the scar from the boar hunt. The old nurse's loyalty becomes the picture's subject — twenty years of absence undone by a touch and a memory.

artworks.title: Ulysses and Eurycleia
artworks.description: Boulanger's academic oil stages the foot-washing in a carefully reconstructed Homeric interior: Eurycleia kneels, the basin between them, as recognition flashes across her face. A Prix de Rome generation's reading of Odyssey 19 — the nurse as the poem's quietest, sharpest witness.

artworks.title: Eurycleia Recognizing Ulysses
artworks.description: A Victorian classicising canvas from the circle of Edward Poynter: Eurycleia starts back as she knows her master by the scar. The scene that Homer keeps almost secret — Odysseus silencing his nurse so the suitors will not hear — becomes a polished gallery drama of loyalty and danger.

artworks.title: Penelope Awakened by Eurycleia with the News of Ulysses' Return
artworks.description: Kauffman shifts the nurse forward to a later beat of the nostos: Eurycleia wakes Penelope with word that Odysseus has returned and the suitors are dead. The old servant who knew the scar becomes the messenger of restored order — Homeric fidelity painted as tender Neoclassical theatre.

popCulture.title: Eurycleia
popCulture.description: The nurse who knows Odysseus by his scar remains the Odyssey's most intimate recognition — loyalty that sees through twenty years' disguise.
